  "summary": "S1 — Fact: The scope is an existing Node.js project with an in-memory user store and an HTTP server; discovery should inspect README.md and src/server.js, then trace the store, routes, package scripts, and tests as unverified leads. Discovery must establish the existing endpoint contract and runtime behavior before selecting compatible changes; this blocks implementation decisions. S2 — Fact: Add name filtering and pagination to the existing user-list HTTP endpoint, with tests; the endpoint and its test suite are the intended places where the result must become usable. Discovery must identify query conventions, response shape, ordering, validation, and test patterns; these answers block the API design and tests. Recorded defaults, used only where discovery finds no established convention: filtering is optional, case-insensitive substring matching; pagination is optional and preserves the current unpaginated response when omitted; discovery must establish the existing contract first and choose compatible parameter names, pagination behavior, and error handling. These defaults rule out requiring pagination or changing existing responses for requests without new parameters. For interaction and state, the API client is the requesting actor; discovery must establish how the runtime identifies callers, whether state is shared across callers, devices, or sessions, how long it lives and what ends it, and what data is hidden from whom. Until established, assume the existing runtime and in-memory store govern these behaviors and add no identity, persistence, or access-control features; these questions block any change that would depend on them. No deployment target is named: the outcome will be visible in the isolated source checkout at final return, while any deployed outcome would exist only after a separate release."
